title: NASA's Swift Telescope Ends 22-Year Mission, Heads For Atmospheric Re-Entry
excerpt: The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory made its final observation on October 20 after atmospheric drag pulled it to 171 miles, ending a two-year mission that lasted more than 10 times as long.
body:
• NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory made its final observation on October 20, 2026, and has ended science operations as its orbit sank to 171 miles (275 km).
  • Launched on November 20, 2004 for a two-year primary mission, Swift worked for more than 10 times as long, observing over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and contributing to about 7,000 scientific papers.
  • Increased solar activity raised atmospheric drag and pulled Swift down rapidly; a high-risk commercial servicing mission ended in August without attempting an orbital boost.
  • The spacecraft is expected to re-enter Earth's atmosphere in the next few weeks, while its 12-terabyte public archive will keep supporting research for decades.

A rapid-response telescope falls silent

NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has concluded operations and is preparing to re-enter Earth's atmosphere, the agency announced on October 23. The spacecraft made its final science observation on October 20, according to NASA's mission-end announcement, after its orbit dropped below 171 miles (275 kilometres) and atmospheric drag made it impossible for its telescopes to hold steady on their targets.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=xixQZ0xjAJg

On October 20 Swift entered safe mode at that altitude. The operations team at Penn State in University Park then sent a command that effectively ended Swift operations to prepare the spacecraft for re-entry, NASA said in its Swift blog update. Re-entry is expected in the next few weeks.

"Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long."

— Shawn Domagal-Goldman, Director, Astrophysics Division, NASA Headquarters

Built to chase the universe's biggest explosions

Swift launched on November 20, 2004, to solve a decades-old problem: gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the cosmos, fade in seconds, and no telescope could locate them fast enough to study their afterglows. Swift was built to detect a burst, pinpoint it, relay its position to other observatories and swing its own co-aligned X-ray and ultraviolet/optical telescopes onto it — typically within about a minute, according to principal investigator S. Bradley Cenko at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center.

The design paid off early. In May 2005 Swift caught GRB 050509B, a short burst lasting just 0.03 seconds, and detected 11 X-ray photons from its afterglow — the first short burst ever located that way. The result supported the theory that short bursts come from mergers of two neutron stars. A flexible target-of-opportunity system later let astronomers request observations within minutes and schedule up to 75 independent targets a day.

A record measured in bursts, supernovae and papers

Over nearly 22 years Swift observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and more than 1,400 supernova explosions. It watched stars being shredded by black holes, monitored active galaxies, completed an all-sky X-ray survey and studied asteroids and comets, NASA said. Data from the mission has contributed to about 7,000 published scientific papers.

The archive it leaves behind holds nearly 22 years of measurements, more than 1.5 million images from its Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope and about 12 terabytes of data — roughly the storage equivalent of 600 high-definition movies — all publicly available. The mission was renamed in 2018 for its first principal investigator, Neil Gehrels, after his death.

Why Swift could not be saved

All satellites in low Earth orbit experience atmospheric drag, and recent solar activity increased that drag on Swift, which began to sink rapidly. NASA paused science observations to minimise drag and preserve time in orbit for a high-risk, fast-turnaround servicing mission intended to boost the observatory. That mission ended in August without an attempt to boost Swift, NASA said.

Swift then restarted observations and studied hundreds of targets in its final weeks, from remnants of stellar explosions to active supermassive black holes and comets in our own solar system. Returning to science increased drag again, and the spacecraft sank quickly to the October 20 threshold where steady pointing was no longer possible.

What happens after Swift

NASA says it will keep prioritising rapid response to cosmic events, using and augmenting its existing fleet of space telescopes while exploring fast-to-orbit commercial capabilities and new missions. For researchers, including the many Indian-origin astronomers working in US and European astrophysics groups, the immediate resource is the open Swift archive, which Domagal-Goldman said "will fuel new discoveries for decades more." The next milestone is the re-entry itself, expected within weeks, which will close a mission that outlived its design life by more than a decade.
